plainLanguage: Year 3. Every digit in a three digit number has a value that depends on its column. In 346 the 3 is worth three hundred, not three.
expectedMethods: Build the number with base ten blocks or place value counters
Partition it out loud as 300 and 40 and 6
Write it in a place value chart with headed columns
parentMethod: Read the digits left to right and say the number.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Counting on and back in steps of 4, 8, 50 and 100, and finding ten or a hundred more or less than a number.
expectedMethods: Jump along a number line in equal steps
Use a hundred square and move a whole row for ten
Say the pattern aloud and notice which digit changes
parentMethod: Add or subtract the number in your head.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Comparing and ordering numbers up to 1000, using the greater than and less than signs.
expectedMethods: Compare the hundreds first, then the tens, then the ones
Place both numbers on a number line and see which is further right
Line the digits up in a place value chart
parentMethod: The bigger number is the one with more digits, or the bigger first digit.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Adding and subtracting in your head with three digit numbers, adding ones, tens or hundreds at a time.
expectedMethods: Add the hundreds, then the tens, then the ones, keeping a running total
Round to a friendly number and adjust at the end
Jump along an empty number line in convenient steps
parentMethod: Write it out in columns even for a mental question.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Column addition and subtraction with up to three digits, including carrying and exchanging.
expectedMethods: Set the digits out in place value columns before calculating
Exchange a ten for ten ones with counters before recording it
Say what is being exchanged rather than just moving a digit
parentMethod: Carry the one, and borrow from next door and pay it back.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Estimating an answer before calculating, and using the opposite operation to check it afterwards.
expectedMethods: Round both numbers and work out roughly what to expect
Check a subtraction by adding the answer back on
Ask whether the answer is sensible before writing it down
parentMethod: Do the sum again and see if you get the same thing.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Knowing the 3, 4 and 8 times tables and the division facts that go with them.
expectedMethods: Double the 2 times table to get 4, and double again for 8
Build the fact as an array of rows and columns
Say the matching division fact straight after the multiplication
parentMethod: Chant the tables until they stick.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Multiplying a two digit number by a one digit number, moving from jottings towards a written method.
expectedMethods: Split the two digit number into tens and ones and multiply each
Draw a grid with the tens and ones along the top
Record the partial answers, then add them
parentMethod: Short multiplication, carrying underneath.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Word problems where something is scaled up, or where every one of a set can be paired with every one of another set.
expectedMethods: Draw a bar model showing one part and how many times bigger the other is
List the pairings systematically rather than at random
Act it out with objects before writing anything
parentMethod: Look for a keyword in the question and pick the operation it suggests.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Tenths. One tenth is what you get when a whole is cut into ten equal parts, or when a number is divided by ten.
expectedMethods: Cut a strip or a circle into ten equal parts and shade some
Count up and down in tenths along a number line
Connect one tenth to dividing by 10
parentMethod: A tenth is 0.1, so move the decimal point.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Finding a fraction of a set of objects, both unit fractions like one third and non unit fractions like two thirds.
expectedMethods: Share the objects into the number of groups the bottom number says
Take as many of those groups as the top number says
Draw the set and ring the groups
parentMethod: Divide by the bottom, times by the top.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Treating a fraction as a number in its own right, with a place on the number line, rather than only as part of a shape.
expectedMethods: Mark the fraction on a number line between 0 and 1
Count on in that fraction past 1
Compare two fractions by their position, not their digits
parentMethod: A fraction is a top number over a bottom number.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Fractions that look different but are the same size, such as one half and two quarters, shown with diagrams.
expectedMethods: Fold or shade two identical strips and compare the shaded amounts
Line up two fraction walls and look for equal lengths
Mark both fractions on the same number line
parentMethod: Multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Adding and subtracting fractions that already have the same bottom number, staying within one whole.
expectedMethods: Shade the pieces on one diagram and count them
Count on in that size of piece along a number line
Say it in words first, as five sevenths plus one seventh
parentMethod: Add the tops and leave the bottom alone.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Measuring, comparing, adding and subtracting lengths in metres, centimetres and millimetres, mass in kilograms and grams, and volume in litres and millilitres.
expectedMethods: Convert both amounts to the same unit before calculating
Read the scale carefully and work out what one interval is worth
Estimate first, then measure
parentMethod: Move the decimal point three places between the units.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Perimeter is the distance all the way round the outside of a shape.
expectedMethods: Mark a starting corner and add the sides going round
Trace round the edge with a finger while counting
Label every side, including the ones not written on the diagram
parentMethod: Add up all the sides.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Telling the time on an analogue clock to the nearest minute, including Roman numerals, and using both 12 hour and 24 hour clocks.
expectedMethods: Read the hour hand first, then count round in fives for the minutes
Use a clock face with movable hands to show the time
Count on in minutes to work out how long something takes
parentMethod: Read the digital clock and subtract twelve if it is past noon.

plainLanguage: Year 3. An angle is an amount of turn. A right angle is a quarter turn, and four of them make a full turn.
expectedMethods: Turn a physical object and count the quarter turns
Compare an angle against the corner of a piece of paper
Sort angles into bigger than, smaller than, or equal to a right angle
parentMethod: A right angle is 90 degrees.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Lines that are horizontal or vertical, lines that meet at a right angle (perpendicular), and lines that never meet (parallel).
expectedMethods: Find examples of each in the room and describe them
Mark parallel lines with arrows and right angles with a square
Test with the corner of a page or a ruler
parentMethod: Parallel lines are the ones that look like train tracks.

plainLanguage: Year 3. Reading and drawing bar charts, pictograms and tables, where one symbol or one square may stand for more than one thing.
expectedMethods: Work out what one interval or one symbol is worth before reading anything off
Answer how many more and how many fewer by comparing two bars
Check the answer against the scale rather than counting squares
parentMethod: Read the number off the axis.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Place value in four digit numbers, up to thousands, and ordering numbers beyond 1000.
expectedMethods: Partition the number into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones
Set it out in a place value chart
Compare digit by digit from the left
parentMethod: Read it out loud and the size is obvious.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Negative numbers, met by counting backwards through zero. Minus five is smaller than minus three, not bigger.
expectedMethods: Count back past zero along a number line that extends both ways
Use a thermometer or a lift as a context
Order a set of negatives by position on the line
parentMethod: Ignore the minus sign and treat it as an ordinary number.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Rounding any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000.
expectedMethods: Find the two multiples the number sits between
Mark it on a number line and see which end is nearer
Look at the digit in the column to the right of the one you are rounding to
parentMethod: Five and above, round up. Four and below, round down.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Reading Roman numerals up to 100, and knowing that the system had no zero and no place value.
expectedMethods: Read left to right, subtracting when a smaller letter comes first
Break the numeral into chunks and total them
Compare a Roman numeral with the same number written in digits
parentMethod: Learn the letters and their values by heart.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Column addition and subtraction with up to four digits, including exchanging across a zero.
expectedMethods: Line the digits up by place value, not by the end of the number
Show the exchange with counters before recording it
Estimate first so a mistake stands out
parentMethod: Borrow from next door, and if it is a zero keep going left.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Two step word problems where you have to decide which operations to use and in what order.
expectedMethods: Draw a bar model showing the parts and the whole
Write down what the first step gives you before starting the second
Say the question back in your own words first
parentMethod: Look for the keywords and do what they say.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Knowing all the times tables up to 12 times 12, and the division facts that come with them. This is the year they are expected to be automatic.
expectedMethods: Practise the facts that are still slow rather than the whole table
Derive a hard fact from an easy one, so 7 times 8 from 7 times 4 doubled
Say the matching division fact immediately after
parentMethod: Chant each table in order from the beginning.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Factor pairs. Two numbers that multiply to make a third are a factor pair of it, and the order they are multiplied in does not matter.
expectedMethods: Work through 1, 2, 3 and so on, testing each in turn
Arrange counters into every possible rectangle
Stop once the pairs start repeating
parentMethod: List the numbers that divide into it.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Short multiplication: multiplying a two or three digit number by a single digit in a formal written layout.
expectedMethods: Split the big number into its parts and multiply each one
Use a grid with the parts along the top before moving to the compact layout
Check the size of the answer against an estimate
parentMethod: Short multiplication with the carried digits tucked underneath.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Breaking a multiplication into easier parts, so 39 times 7 becomes 30 times 7 plus 9 times 7.
expectedMethods: Partition one number and multiply each part separately
Show it as two rectangles side by side
Add the partial answers at the end
parentMethod: Just do the standard written method.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Families of equivalent fractions, and simplifying by spotting a common factor, so six ninths is two thirds.
expectedMethods: Line up fraction strips and look for equal lengths
Find a number that divides into both the top and the bottom
Mark the family on one number line
parentMethod: Cancel down by dividing top and bottom.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Hundredths. One hundredth is a whole cut into a hundred parts, or a tenth cut into ten.
expectedMethods: Shade a hundred square and name the amount
Divide a tenth strip into ten and name one piece
Count up and down in hundredths
parentMethod: A hundredth is 0.01, two places after the point.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Writing tenths and hundredths as decimals, and knowing the decimal equivalents of a quarter, a half and three quarters.
expectedMethods: Shade the same amount on a hundred square and a fraction strip
Place the fraction and the decimal at the same point on a number line
Say it as seventy one hundredths as well as nought point seven one
parentMethod: Divide the top by the bottom on a calculator.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Dividing a number by 10 or 100 and seeing the digits move into the tenths and hundredths columns.
expectedMethods: Move the digits along a place value chart and keep the point still
Say what each digit is worth after the move
Check against an estimate of the size
parentMethod: Move the decimal point one place for each zero.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Comparing decimals with the same number of decimal places, and rounding a decimal with one place to the nearest whole number.
expectedMethods: Compare the whole numbers first, then the tenths, then the hundredths
Place both on a number line between two whole numbers
Line the decimal points up underneath each other
parentMethod: The longer decimal is the bigger one.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Converting between units of measure, such as kilometres to metres or hours to minutes.
expectedMethods: Decide first whether the answer should be bigger or smaller
Multiply going to a smaller unit, divide going to a larger one
Write the conversion fact down before starting
parentMethod: Move the decimal point the right number of places.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Perimeter of a shape made only of straight lines and right angles, including working out sides that are not labelled.
expectedMethods: Work out the missing sides from the ones you are given
Mark each side as you add it so none is counted twice
Check that opposite sides of the whole shape total the same
parentMethod: Add up all the sides, or use two times length plus width.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Area, introduced by counting the squares that cover a shape rather than by a formula.
expectedMethods: Count the squares inside the shape one at a time
Notice the squares make rows that are all the same size
Connect the count to multiplying rows by columns
parentMethod: Length times width.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Reading and converting between 12 hour and 24 hour clocks, and solving problems about how long something lasts.
expectedMethods: Count on to the next whole hour first, then on to the end time
Use a blank number line to record the jumps
Add twelve to the hours for afternoon times
parentMethod: Subtract the start time from the end time in columns.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Sorting triangles and quadrilaterals by their properties, so equilateral, isosceles and scalene, or parallelogram, rhombus and trapezium.
expectedMethods: Check the sides and the angles, not just the overall look
Sort a set of shapes and say what rule was used
Test whether a shape can belong to more than one group
parentMethod: Recognise the shape by its name and picture.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Acute angles are smaller than a right angle and obtuse angles are bigger, and angles can be put in order by size.
expectedMethods: Compare each angle against a right angle corner
Order a set of angles without measuring them
Notice that the length of the arms does not change the angle
parentMethod: Acute is under 90, obtuse is over 90.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Lines of symmetry in two dimensional shapes, including shapes that are not the right way up, and completing a symmetric figure.
expectedMethods: Fold or use a mirror to test a line
Count corresponding points the same distance from the line
Turn the shape round and check the line still works
parentMethod: A line of symmetry cuts it down the middle.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Coordinates in the first quadrant, written as a pair, and describing a move as so many left or right and so many up or down.
expectedMethods: Read along the bottom first, then up
Plot the points and join them to complete a shape
Describe a translation in both directions separately
parentMethod: Along the corridor and up the stairs.

plainLanguage: Year 4. Bar charts and time graphs, and answering comparison, total and difference questions from them.
expectedMethods: Work out what one interval on the axis is worth first
Read both values before comparing them
Decide whether the question wants a total or a difference
parentMethod: Read the numbers off the graph.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Reading, writing, ordering and comparing numbers up to a million, and knowing what each digit is worth.
expectedMethods: Group the digits in threes to read the number
Use a place value chart with a thousands column
Compare from the leftmost digit
parentMethod: Count the digits to see how big it is.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Negative numbers in real contexts, counting forwards and backwards through zero.
expectedMethods: Use a number line that runs both sides of zero
Count the distance to zero and then onwards
Use temperature or money owed as the context
parentMethod: Two minuses make a plus.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Rounding any number up to a million to the nearest 10, 100, 1000, 10 000 or 100 000.
expectedMethods: Identify the two multiples the number sits between
Underline the digit in the column you are rounding to
Look only at the digit immediately to its right
parentMethod: Five or more, round up.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Column addition and subtraction with numbers of more than four digits, and multi step problems where you choose the operations.
expectedMethods: Estimate by rounding before calculating
Line the digits up by place value
Write down what each step has found before moving on
parentMethod: Carry and borrow in columns.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Factors and multiples, including all the factor pairs of a number and the factors two numbers share.
expectedMethods: Test 1, 2, 3 and so on in order until the pairs meet
List the factors of both numbers and look for the ones in both
Use arrays to show why a pair works
parentMethod: Write out the times tables and see what appears.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Prime numbers have exactly two factors, one and themselves. Numbers with more than two are composite.
expectedMethods: Test divisibility by 2, 3, 5 and 7 in turn
Try to build a rectangle other than a single row
Recall the primes up to 19 by heart
parentMethod: A prime is one that only divides by itself and one.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Long multiplication: multiplying a number of up to four digits by a two digit number in a formal written layout.
expectedMethods: Multiply by the ones, then by the tens, then add the two rows
Put a zero as a place holder on the second row and say why it is there
Estimate the answer first by rounding both numbers
parentMethod: Long multiplication, with a zero on the second line.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Short division by a single digit, and deciding what to do with a remainder depending on the question.
expectedMethods: Carry the remainder into the next column as a small digit
Decide whether the context needs a remainder, a fraction, a decimal or rounding
Check by multiplying the answer back
parentMethod: The bus stop method, and write r for the remainder.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1000, including with decimals.
expectedMethods: Move the digits along the place value chart and keep the point fixed
Say how many places and in which direction before moving anything
Check that the answer got bigger or smaller as expected
parentMethod: Move the decimal point, or add a zero.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Square numbers and cube numbers, and the notation for squared and cubed.
expectedMethods: Build the square as a square array of counters
Build the cube as a cube of blocks
Learn the squares up to 12 as facts
parentMethod: Squared means times itself.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Comparing and ordering fractions whose bottom numbers are multiples of the same number.
expectedMethods: Change them to a common bottom number, then compare the tops
Place them all on one number line
Compare each against a half as a benchmark
parentMethod: Cross multiply and compare.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Mixed numbers and improper fractions, and converting between them, so six fifths is one and one fifth.
expectedMethods: Shade whole shapes and a part to show the mixed number
Count on in fifths past one on a number line
Connect it to dividing the top by the bottom
parentMethod: Divide the top by the bottom and the remainder is the fraction.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Adding and subtracting fractions where one bottom number is a multiple of the other, by making the pieces the same size first.
expectedMethods: Change only the fraction that needs changing
Draw both fractions and cut the pieces so they match
Say why the bottom number stays the same once they match
parentMethod: Find a common denominator, then add the tops.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Multiplying a fraction or a mixed number by a whole number, supported by diagrams.
expectedMethods: Show it as repeated addition of the same fraction
Draw the fraction the right number of times and total the pieces
Convert an improper answer back to a mixed number
parentMethod: Times the top and leave the bottom.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Decimals to three places, including thousandths, and reading, ordering and rounding them.
expectedMethods: Use a place value chart with tenths, hundredths and thousandths
Compare place by place from the left
Place the number on a number line between two whole numbers
parentMethod: Line the decimal points up and compare.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Per cent means parts per hundred. Fifty per cent is fifty hundredths, a half, or 0.5.
expectedMethods: Shade a hundred square to show the percentage
Write it as a fraction over a hundred and simplify
Learn the common equivalents for a half, a quarter and fifths
parentMethod: Move the decimal point two places to turn a percentage into a decimal.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Converting between metric units, and knowing roughly how they compare with inches, pounds and pints.
expectedMethods: Decide whether the number should get bigger or smaller first
Use the place value chart rather than a remembered rule
Check the answer is a sensible size in real terms
parentMethod: Times or divide by a thousand and move the point.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Area of rectangles in square centimetres and square metres, and estimating the area of irregular shapes.
expectedMethods: Split a composite shape into rectangles and total the areas
Count whole squares and pair up the part squares for an estimate
Keep both measurements in the same unit before multiplying
parentMethod: Length times width.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Perimeter of composite shapes made from rectangles, including finding lengths that are not marked.
expectedMethods: Work out the unmarked sides from the ones you are given
Go round once, marking each side as it is added
Check opposite sides of the bounding rectangle match
parentMethod: Add all the sides up.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Measuring and drawing angles in degrees with a protractor, including reflex angles over 180 degrees.
expectedMethods: Line the centre of the protractor on the point and the zero on one arm
Decide first whether the angle is acute or obtuse, then pick the right scale
Extend a short arm so it reaches the scale
parentMethod: Put the protractor on and read the number.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Angles round a point total 360 degrees and angles on a straight line total 180, which lets you find a missing one.
expectedMethods: Write the total down first, then subtract the known angles
Mark the angles that make the whole turn or the straight line
Check the answer looks the right size on the diagram
parentMethod: Subtract from 180 or 360.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Reflecting and translating a shape, and knowing the shape itself does not change size or form.
expectedMethods: Measure each point's distance from the mirror line and match it
Move every vertex by the same amount for a translation
Check the reflected shape is the same size, not a different one
parentMethod: Flip it over, or slide it across.

plainLanguage: Year 5. Reading line graphs and timetables, and answering comparison, total and difference questions from them.
expectedMethods: Work out the scale on both axes before reading anything
Track across and down to read a point accurately
Read a timetable by following one column down
parentMethod: Find it on the graph and read it off.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Reading, writing, ordering and comparing numbers up to ten million, and rounding any of them to a stated accuracy.
expectedMethods: Group the digits in threes to read the number aloud
Compare from the leftmost digit
Underline the rounding column and check the digit to its right
parentMethod: Count the commas and read it off.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Negative numbers in context, and working out the gap between a negative and a positive number.
expectedMethods: Count up to zero first, then on to the other number
Use a number line running both sides of zero
Use temperature change as the context
parentMethod: Subtract and change the sign.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Long multiplication of a number up to four digits by a two digit number.
expectedMethods: Multiply by the ones, then by the tens, then add the rows
Explain why the second row starts with a zero rather than just writing one
Estimate first so a misplaced row shows up
parentMethod: Long multiplication with a zero on the second line.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Long division by a two digit number, and interpreting the remainder as a remainder, a fraction, a decimal or by rounding.
expectedMethods: Write out the first few multiples of the divisor before starting
Subtract each chunk and bring the next digit down
Decide what the context needs done with the remainder
parentMethod: Long division, or the bus stop method if it fits.

plainLanguage: Year 6. The order of operations, including brackets. Two plus one times three is five, but with brackets round the two plus one it is nine.
expectedMethods: Do the brackets first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract
Rewrite the calculation after each step rather than doing it all at once
Test the same numbers with and without brackets to see the difference
parentMethod: BODMAS.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Common factors, common multiples and prime numbers, used to simplify and to find common denominators.
expectedMethods: List the factors or multiples of both and look for shared ones
Use prime factors to find the highest common factor
Connect a common multiple to a common denominator
parentMethod: Write out both times tables and look for a match.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Simplifying a fraction using a common factor, and rewriting fractions so they share a bottom number.
expectedMethods: Find the highest number that divides into both top and bottom
Use a common multiple of both bottom numbers
Check the simplified fraction sits at the same point on a number line
parentMethod: Cancel down until it will not go any further.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Adding and subtracting fractions with different bottom numbers, and with mixed numbers, by making the pieces the same size first.
expectedMethods: Find a common multiple of both bottom numbers
Draw both fractions and cut them so the pieces match
Deal with the whole numbers separately from the fraction parts
parentMethod: Find the lowest common denominator, then add the tops.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Multiplying two proper fractions, which gives an answer smaller than either of them.
expectedMethods: Shade one fraction of a rectangle, then that fraction of the shaded part
Multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms, then simplify
Notice the answer is smaller and say why
parentMethod: Times the tops, times the bottoms.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Dividing a proper fraction by a whole number, so a third shared between two people is a sixth each.
expectedMethods: Draw the fraction and cut each piece into the number of shares
Say what one share is worth of the original whole
Connect it to multiplying by a unit fraction
parentMethod: Turn it upside down and multiply.

plainLanguage: Year 6. A fraction is also a division, so three eighths is three divided by eight, which is 0.375.
expectedMethods: Divide the top by the bottom using short division
Recall the common equivalents rather than calculating every time
Round a recurring decimal to a sensible number of places
parentMethod: Put it in a calculator.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Moving freely between fractions, decimals and percentages, because they are three ways of saying the same proportion.
expectedMethods: Go through a hundredth as the common step between the three
Learn the common set for halves, quarters, fifths and tenths
Show all three on the same bar or number line
parentMethod: Over a hundred for a percentage, divide for a decimal.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Ratio compares two quantities by how many times bigger one is, not by how much bigger. Two to three scales up to four to six, not three to four.
expectedMethods: Draw a bar model with one bar per part
Find what one part is worth, then scale up
Check by comparing the two quantities as a multiplication
parentMethod: Cross multiply.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Finding a percentage of an amount, and using percentages to compare two things.
expectedMethods: Find ten per cent first, then build the rest from it
Draw a bar split into ten or a hundred parts
Find one per cent when the percentage is awkward
parentMethod: Divide by a hundred and times by the percentage.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Scale factor, and problems about similar shapes where one is an enlargement of the other.
expectedMethods: Compare one pair of matching sides to find the factor
Apply the same factor to every length
Check that the angles have not changed
parentMethod: Divide the new by the old.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Unequal sharing, such as splitting an amount so one person gets three parts for every two the other gets.
expectedMethods: Count the total number of parts first
Divide the total by the number of parts to find one part
Draw a bar model showing the parts side by side
parentMethod: Split it in the ratio given.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Using a simple formula, where a letter stands for a number that can change.
expectedMethods: Say the formula in words before using symbols
Substitute the value and work through one step at a time
Use a familiar rule such as perimeter or area as the example
parentMethod: Put the numbers in and work it out.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Number sequences that go up or down by the same amount each time, and describing the rule.
expectedMethods: Find the difference between consecutive terms
Describe the rule in words before writing it with a letter
Test the rule on a term further along
parentMethod: Spot the pattern and carry it on.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Writing a missing number problem with a letter, and finding pairs of numbers that fit an equation with two unknowns.
expectedMethods: Replace the empty box with a letter and keep the rest the same
Work backwards using the opposite operation
List the possible pairs in order rather than guessing
parentMethod: Move it to the other side and change the sign.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Converting between units of length, mass, volume and time using decimals, and between miles and kilometres.
expectedMethods: Decide first whether the number should get bigger or smaller
Use the place value chart rather than a remembered rule
Use the rough five miles to eight kilometres relationship to check
parentMethod: Multiply or divide by a thousand.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Area of parallelograms and triangles, and the fact that shapes with the same area can have different perimeters.
expectedMethods: Cut and rearrange a parallelogram into a rectangle
See a triangle as half of a rectangle around it
Use the perpendicular height, not the slanted side
parentMethod: Half base times height.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Volume of cubes and cuboids in cubic centimetres and cubic metres.
expectedMethods: Build the cuboid from unit cubes and count a layer
Multiply one layer by the number of layers
Keep all three measurements in the same unit
parentMethod: Length times width times height.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Finding unknown angles in triangles, quadrilaterals and regular polygons using the angle totals.
expectedMethods: Write the total for the shape first, then subtract the known angles
Split a polygon into triangles to find its total
Use the properties of the shape, such as equal angles in an isosceles triangle
parentMethod: Angles in a triangle add to 180.

plainLanguage: Year 6. The parts of a circle: radius, diameter and circumference, and that the diameter is twice the radius.
expectedMethods: Label a drawn circle with all three parts
Fold a paper circle to find the diameter and then the radius
Use the doubling and halving relationship both ways
parentMethod: Diameter is twice the radius.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Angles that meet at a point, sit on a straight line, or are vertically opposite when two lines cross.
expectedMethods: Mark which angles make the full turn or the straight line
Identify the vertically opposite pair and say they are equal
Write the total down before subtracting
parentMethod: Opposite angles are equal, angles on a line add to 180.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Coordinates in all four quadrants, including negative ones, and translating or reflecting a shape on the grid.
expectedMethods: Read along the x axis first, then up or down the y axis
Move every vertex by the same amount and rejoin them
Predict a missing coordinate from the properties of the shape
parentMethod: Along the corridor and up the stairs, minus for the other side.

plainLanguage: Year 6. Pie charts and line graphs, where the whole circle is 360 degrees and each slice is a share of it.
expectedMethods: Connect each slice to a fraction or percentage of the whole
Work out what one part is worth before reading individual slices
Read a line graph by tracking across and down to the axes
parentMethod: Read the labels on the chart.

plainLanguage: Year 6. The mean, found by totalling the values and dividing by how many there are, and knowing when it is a sensible thing to use.
expectedMethods: Level out a set of towers of cubes so they are all equal
Total the values and divide by the count
Include every value, including any zeros
parentMethod: Add them up and divide by how many.
